prerequisites.meaning: A measure of how changing a quantity would change a loss.
prerequisites.check: Why must a generator receive feedback about its output to improve?
prerequisites.answer: Without feedback on its own output, it cannot tell which weight changes would make its images more realistic.

diagrams.title: A GAN learns from a discriminator
diagrams.subtitle: Two networks learn different tasks; only the generator creates new images.

trace: A real MNIST batch is scaled to [−1, 1]; G receives separate Gaussian codes of length 64.
G upsamples each code through 7×7, 14×14, and 28×28 feature grids.
D scores real images and detached fake images; opt_D updates D using source labels.
The original connected fakes pass through updated D; opt_G improves their real-labelled score.
After training, draw new codes and use G alone; inspect both image quality and diversity.
diagrams.explanation: A generative adversarial network, or GAN, contains two networks with different jobs. The generator G transforms a random latent code into an image. The discriminator D judges whether an image came from the dataset or the generator. Real images follow a separate path into D; they do not pass through G. Training alternates two updates. The discriminator learns to assign real labels to dataset images and fake labels to generated ones. The generator then learns to make its images receive the real label from the updated discriminator. Gradients from D guide G even though G never receives a matching target digit for each noise code. This creates a moving learning problem: improving either network changes the other network's task. Loss curves alone cannot show success. The lab compares fixed-code snapshots, predicted digit coverage, and a custom feature distance. Generation after training needs G and a fresh code, without D.
diagrams.check_question: Which networks must run to generate a new digit after training?
diagrams.check_answer: Only G is needed. D supplied training feedback but is not part of the generation path.

diagrams.title: One alternating GAN update
diagrams.subtitle: Detach fakes for the D update; keep G connected for its own update.
diagrams.feedback: Updated G makes the next batch’s fake images.
trace: Suppose D confidently rejects a generated digit; that creates a large real-target generator cost.
During the D step, fake.detach blocks gradients from reaching G through that loss.
During the G step, g_loss_fn uses the original fake so gradients can travel through D to G.
opt_G steps G's parameters; the discriminator is a scoring route rather than the optimiser target.
diagrams.explanation: The important distinction is between a tensor's values and its gradient connection. The call fake.detach() supplies the same image values to D while cutting the route back to G for that operation. This lets the discriminator learn from generated images without updating the generator from the discriminator's loss. The original fake tensor remains connected to G. After opt_D changes D's weights, g_loss_fn sends that original tensor through D and asks for the real label. This non-saturating generator objective rewards fakes that D accepts. Backpropagation follows the chain from the loss through D's operations, through the fake image, and into G's weights. The optimiser step then changes only the parameters registered with opt_G. The labels therefore serve different purposes in the two updates: fake means 0 when training D, but G's desired target is 1. Repeat this sequence for each training batch.
diagrams.check_question: Why would detaching fake inside g_loss_fn stop the generator from learning?
diagrams.check_answer: It would cut the gradient path from the generator loss back to G's weights.

diagrams.title: Train, inspect, and evaluate a GAN
diagrams.subtitle: Check visual quality and coverage with evidence beyond the training loss.
trace: Reuse z_fixed across epoch snapshots so image changes reflect training rather than new noise inputs.
Compare lerp and slerp images and midpoint norms; neither path guarantees valid digits.
Check the classifier's test accuracy before trusting its histogram of 2,000 generated digits.
Compare real-versus-real, epoch-1, final, and uniform-noise feature distances using the same clf.
On the eight-cluster ring, inspect both the scatter plots and modes_covered for each trained system.
diagrams.explanation: The lab asks two separate evaluation questions: do the images resemble digits, and does the generator cover varied digits? Fixed-noise snapshots answer a visual progress question because each epoch uses the same input codes. The digit classifier estimates class coverage, but its mistakes can distort the histogram, so first check its test accuracy and inspect samples. Its hidden features also define a custom Fréchet distance. This compares two sets of feature vectors through their means and covariance matrices; it is not the standard Inception-based FID. Real-versus-real features provide a reference for finite-sample differences. Keep the feature network, preprocessing, and sample count fixed when comparing generators. The toy ring makes missing modes easy to see. WGAN-GP changes the scoring objective and adds a gradient penalty, so its training feedback differs from ordinary real/fake classification. Better toy coverage is evidence for that experiment, not a guarantee for every dataset.
diagrams.check_question: Can a low feature distance alone prove that every digit class is represented?
diagrams.check_answer: No. Inspect the coverage histogram and samples as well; the feature statistic summarises only some aspects of the distribution.

diagrams.title: Where the GAN training feedback comes from
diagrams.subtitle: Real images train the discriminator. Its feedback trains the generator.

steps.title: Get real and fake
steps.detail: Real data; G makes a fake batch.

steps.title: Recheck linked fakes
steps.detail: Updated D passes feedback to G.

diagrams.explanation: A GAN has two losses and two weight updates. First, D learns to label real images as 1 and generated images as 0. The fake images are detached during this step so its loss does not update G. Next, updated D rates fake images that still have a gradient path back to G. The generator loss uses target 1: it asks G to make images D accepts as real. Only G's optimiser takes a step here. Fixed-noise snapshots show how those updates changed the generated images.
trace: If D gives a fake image probability 0.1, the generator's non-saturating loss is −ln(0.1), about 2.30.
If it instead gives 0.8, the generator cost is about 0.22.
G learns changes that make D's fake score higher. D learns changes that separate the two sources.
A falling loss alone cannot show whether all digit classes are covered.
diagrams.check_question: Why is the generator target 1 for a fake image?
diagrams.check_answer: Target 1 expresses G's goal: make D accept its image as real. The discriminator still uses target 0 for fakes in its own update.
diagrams.feedback: Repeat both weight updates with a fresh batch.

diagrams.title: Use the trained generator on new noise
diagrams.insert_before_title: Real DCGAN samples across training epochs
diagrams.subtitle: After training, the generator can create images without a discriminator call.
diagrams.explanation: The generator is the part needed to create new images. It takes fresh random codes and runs one forward pass through its learned layers. The discriminator supplied training feedback, but it does not need to run during generation. Evaluation mode matters because layers such as batch normalisation should use their stored statistics. Compare many samples for quality and variety. A sharp-looking sample can still come from a model that only makes a few digit classes. Use the same noise codes when comparing two saved generator versions.
trace: One random code has Z_DIM = 64 values in this lab.
A batch of 16 codes produces 16 digit images.
Reuse the same 16 codes after different epochs to see the effect of training.
Count predicted classes over a larger batch to look for missing digits.
diagrams.check_question: Which network is needed to create a new image after training?
diagrams.check_answer: The trained generator G. D is used for learning feedback, while separate evaluation checks can measure the resulting samples.

glossary.meaning: A network that transforms a random code into a generated example.
A network trained to distinguish dataset examples from generated examples.
An unnormalised classification score; sigmoid turns a binary logit into a probability.
Keep tensor values while disconnecting their gradient path for an operation.
The generator objective that asks D to label generated samples as real.
A generator produces only a small part of the variety present in the training distribution.
A numerical representation extracted from an intermediate layer of a network.
A training cost encouraging the critic's input-gradient norm to stay near one on sampled interpolates.

pitfalls: A discriminator output near 0.5 can reflect balance or poor learning; inspect images and coverage as well.
A generator does not reconstruct the corresponding real training image for each random code.
The DigitCNN feature distance has its own scale and cannot be directly compared with reported Inception FID values.

recap.example: Illustrative G loss: if D(fake) = 0.1, −ln(0.1) ≈ 2.30; at 0.8 it is ≈ 0.22.
recap.question: Why must fake stay linked to G during the generator update?
recap.answer: Gradients must travel from its loss through D and the fake image to G’s weights.
recap.next: In Week 4 we learn from known noise targets and generate by repeated denoising.
recap.notes: Ask two students to narrate the two update roles. One explains D’s real and fake labels; the other explains why G’s target for its fake image is one. Use the illustrative loss values to show what the generator wants without mistaking loss size for image quality. Point out that detach preserves pixel values while cutting a gradient route. Ask the exit question before showing the answer. Then show two equally sharp digit samples of the same class and ask why sharpness alone cannot demonstrate coverage. Close with one provenance or disclosure action and connect the next week to a fixed regression target.
